Gravity mg has a component mg sin(θ) along the arc. This is the restoring force: F = -mg sin(θ) ≈ -mgθ for small angles.

t: The pull back to the middle is called the restoring force. It is zero at the middle and strongest at the edges.
The pull back to the middle is called the restoring force. It gets stronger the further you are from the centre.
The restoring force is what makes things oscillate. For a pendulum, it is gravity pulling the bob back toward the lowest point. The further from the centre, the stronger the pull.

The restoring force is F = -mg sin(θ) for a pendulum. It is a function of displacement, zero at equilibrium, maximum at the turning points. The negative sign indicates it opposes the displacement — the defining property of a restoring force.
sub: Without a restoring force, nothing oscillates. With one, things swing back and forth on their own.
A restoring force is what turns a push into a swing. Without it, the push would just... go. With it, the push comes back.
Restoring force → acceleration toward equilibrium → overshoot → restoring force again → oscillation. The cycle is the oscillation.
A restoring force F(x) with F(0)=0 and F'(0)<0 produces oscillation about x=0. For small displacements, F ≈ -kx, giving SHM with ω = √(k/m).

t: Every clock that ticks, every string that vibrates, every bridge that sways — all of them have a restoring force.
Clocks, guitar strings, bridges, swings — all oscillate because something pulls them back to the middle.
Every oscillator in physics — pendulum, spring, LC circuit, atom — has a restoring force. It is the universal mechanism of periodic motion.

The restoring force is the defining feature of every harmonic system: mechanical, electrical, quantum. The harmonic oscillator is the most-solved problem in physics precisely because restoring forces are everywhere.

q: Define the restoring force in an oscillating system.
options: A force that pulls things back toward the middle
A force that pushes things away
A force that stops things from moving
why: A restoring force pulls things back toward the middle. On a swing, gravity does it. The further you are from the middle, the harder it pulls.
A restoring force always points toward the equilibrium position. For a pendulum, gravity's component along the arc does this. Zero at the centre, maximum at the edges.
A restoring force opposes displacement from equilibrium. F(0) = 0, and F points toward 0 for x ≠ 0. This is what produces oscillation.
A restoring force satisfies F(x)·x < 0 (opposes displacement). For small displacements, F ≈ -kx, giving simple harmonic motion with ω² = k/m.

q: Where is the restoring force on a pendulum the strongest?
Where is the restoring force maximum on a pendulum?
At what displacement is the restoring force on a pendulum largest?
For a pendulum, at what θ is |F_restoring| maximised?
options: At the edges — when it is furthest from the middle
At the bottom — when it is moving fastest
The force is the same everywhere
why: The further from the middle, the harder gravity pulls back. At the edges (the turning points), the bob is furthest from centre, so the restoring force is strongest. At the bottom, it is zero.
F = -mg sin(θ). The force is proportional to sin(θ), which is maximum at the largest angle (the turning points) and zero at θ=0 (the bottom).
F_restoring = -mg sin(θ). Maximum |F| at maximum |θ| — the turning points. Zero at θ=0.
F = -mg sin(θ). d|F|/dθ = mg cos(θ) > 0 for |θ| < π/2, so |F| increases with |θ|. Maximum at the amplitude extremes.
